findings.exactExcerpt: The etymology is a compound built from two elements. *Huios* (υἱός) means “my firstborn” — the standard Greek word for son, treated at length in [Hyios](/greek/hyios/).
findings.problem: The gloss says υἱός (huios) means “my firstborn.” υἱός means “son”; it does not mean “my firstborn” (that would be πρωτότοκος, the subject of the prototokos entry). The error contradicts the very next clause in the same sentence (“the standard Greek word for son”), the word-family list a few lines below (“*Huios* (υἱός) — son”), and the linked Hyios entry. The same “my firstborn” substitution recurs at line 133 (“Israel as God’s ‘my firstborn’ (Exodus 4:22, BSB)”) and line 173 (“The Pauline use of ‘my firstborn’ language”), suggesting a mechanical replacement gone wrong; only the line-43 gloss is flatly false, but all three should be reviewed together.

localEvidence.observation: Gloss “my firstborn” for υἱός contradicted in the same sentence and by the family list (“*Huios* (υἱός) — son”) at line 47.
Two further “my firstborn” substitutions in the same article.
πρωτότοκος is the entry glossed “firstborn”; likely source of the carry-over.

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Replace “means “my firstborn”” with “means “son”” at line 43 (and review the “my firstborn” wording at lines 133 and 173).
findings.notes: Internal packet evidence is sufficient; no external authority needed.

findings.exactExcerpt: The three-clause structure is precise. First clause: *en archē ēn ho logos* — "in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."
findings.problem: The English gloss attached to the first clause of John 1:1 (*en archē ēn ho logos*) reproduces the entire verse — all three clauses — instead of just the first clause (“In the beginning was the Word”). The following sentences gloss the second and third clauses separately, so the first gloss silently duplicates their content and undermines the clause-by-clause grammatical analysis the paragraph is making.

localEvidence.observation: First-clause gloss contains the whole of John 1:1; second and third clauses are then glossed separately in the same sentence.
The companion Logos entry treats “the opening five Greek words” (en archē ēn ho logos) as the Genesis 1:1 echo, confirming the intended first-clause scope.

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Change the first-clause gloss to "in the beginning was the Word."
findings.notes: Purely internal inconsistency between the Greek quoted and the English gloss supplied for it.

findings.exactExcerpt: The reconstructed Proto-Indo-European form is *pH₂tér-, and it surfaces in nearly every IE language family with remarkably little change: Latin *pater*, Sanskrit *pitár-*, Persian *pidar*, German *Vater*, English *father*.
findings.problem: Unclosed italics: the asterisk before *pH₂tér- is never closed, so the line has an odd asterisk count. localEvidence.observation: Odd asterisk count on the line; “*pH₂tér-,” lacks its closing asterisk (compare the correctly marked “*pitár-*” later in the same sentence).

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Change “*pH₂tér-,” to “*pH₂tér*-,” (closing the italic span before the hyphen).
findings.notes: Only asterisk-balance defect found in the 250-article scan.

findings.exactExcerpt: Three phrases echo the Old Testament: "my Son" (Psalm 2:7), "the beloved" (the Aqedah of Genesis 22, the only-beloved Isaac), and “And a voice from heaven said, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased!’” (Isaiah 42:1, the chosen servant).
findings.problem: The third “phrase” said to echo Isaiah 42:1 is not a phrase from Isaiah — it is the entire Matthew 3:17 sentence as quoted earlier in the paragraph (including the narrative frame “And a voice from heaven said”). Presenting the whole Matthean sentence as the wording of Isaiah 42:1 misleads the reader about what Isaiah says; the actual echo is the clause “in whom I am well pleased” (compare Isaiah 42:1, “in whom My soul delights” — noting Matthew is echoing, not quoting, Isaiah).

localEvidence.observation: The first two echoes are quoted as short phrases; the third quotes the whole verse, frame included, and labels it “(Isaiah 42:1 …)”.

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Change the third item to quote only the echo phrase, e.g.: and “in whom I am well pleased” (Isaiah 42:1, the chosen servant).
findings.notes: Internal evidence suffices: the quoted wording is demonstrably Matthew 3:17's, repeated from earlier in the same paragraph.

findings.exactExcerpt: Where verses 44 and 46 are printed, the warning recurs after each of the first two sayings and again at the end. Where they are not, it comes once, at verse 47's conclusion.
findings.problem: In the editions without verses 44 and 46 (BSB, BLB, Nestle 1904), the warning about the worm and the fire stands at Mark 9:48, not “at verse 47's conclusion.” Verse 47 in those editions is the saying about the eye. The unit's own sourceObservation says the text runs “from verse 45 to verse 47” and that the line “is identical in wording to Mark 9:48, which every edition here prints”; the companion unit candidate-07 states the fixed point explicitly: “At Mark 9:48, in all seven editions compared here, stands the warning about the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched.” The verse number in the interpretation is wrong.

findings.exactExcerpt: Within these twelve verses the publishers record a remarkable number of small differences — the Majority Standard Bible has twelve textual notes and one rendering note, while the Berean Standard Bible has three textual notes and one rendering note, naming a range of printed editions that read differently at one point or another [C3]. These seventeen Berean notes concern the wording and its rendering, rather than the inclusion of the whole passage.
findings.problem: “These seventeen Berean notes” misattributes the notes. By the sentence's own breakdown, twelve textual notes plus one rendering note belong to the Majority Standard Bible (13) and three textual plus one rendering note to the Berean Standard Bible (4). The total is indeed 17 (12+1+3+1), but only four of them are Berean notes; thirteen are MSB notes. Publisher attribution is exactly the kind of distinction this corpus is careful to preserve, so the label should not lump MSB's notes under “Berean.”

localEvidence.observation: Same sentence allocates 13 notes to MSB and 4 to BSB before calling all seventeen “Berean notes.”
Publisher-attributed claims must remain attributed to the correct publisher; MSB is majoritybible.com, not a Berean edition.

findings.suggestedMinimalCorrection: Change “These seventeen Berean notes” to “These seventeen publisher notes” (or “These seventeen notes”).
